items.headline: Anthropic launches its IPO roadshow
items.summary: Anthropic said it has launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering; its registration statement is filed with the SEC but not yet effective. @ParadisLabs flagged an $81B annual revenue run-rate as of Oct. 31, up $10B (14.1%) from September, while @jukan05 noted the company is pressing ahead even with its valuation cut in half from $2 trillion. @jimcramer called it the most consequential deal of our time, one the Jensen Huang story is obscuring.

items.headline: Report: Huang relationship tied to at least $7.5B in Nvidia chip shipments
items.summary: Citing The Information, @KobeissiLetter reported that Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, said to date back to 2023, facilitated at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments. A day earlier @GavinSBaker argued that since mid-2025 it has increasingly been Beijing, not Washington, blocking Nvidia GPUs in China.
items.short: New report sizes the Huang affair at $7.5B in shipments.

items.headline: SoftBank’s CFO denies it defaulted on data-center turbine orders
items.summary: Asked about Elon Musk’s claim last week that SoftBank was defaulting on turbine orders, CFO Yoshimitsu Goto said it is “simply not correct at all. There is no such default,” @aleabitoreddit reported, noting GE’s CEO has also said he sees no cancellations. @rdd147 had argued the reported defaults spelled trouble for Anthropic’s compute commitments.

items.headline: Musk: Starlink’s network software turns out to suit training superintelligence
items.summary: Elon Musk wrote that the software built to move vast amounts of data through space and down to the ground is also very well suited to training super intelligence, his most-engaged post in the feed this morning.
items.short: Starlink software repurposed for AI training.

items.author: Fireside Alpha
items.text:
JUST IN: Memphis Mayor reveals SpaceX data center taxes more than doubled to $54 million, after $25 million last year made it Shelby County’s second largest taxpayer

Paul Young was asked about Elon Musk’s claim that data centers have Memphis booming:

Q: “Recently, just speaking on the revenues the data centers are creating for Memphis. Elon Musk recently tweeted that Memphis is 'booming' because of the data centers. He said that hotels and restaurants are full and called, tax revenue in Memphis tremendous right now. Do you just have any thoughts on that?”

YOUNG: “Well, we’ve talked a lot about the financial aspects of the project. I think that as we talk about data centers in our city, we want to talk about it in a balanced way. Of course there’s an economic side. We want to make sure that we are articulating what protections and guardrails we’re putting in place for the environmental sides that, people are concerned about, the quality of life, noise, traffic, all of those aspects."

"But, there there is tax revenue. I think this year it was $54,000,000 in taxes that have been generated. And I know last year when they generated about $25,000,000 in tax revenue, it was the second largest tax paying property in Shelby County. I don’t know where $54,000,000 puts it, but it is significant taxes."

"And so as we look at, the tax revenue, we also wanna look at how do we ensure that there are proper protections. That’s what this ninety day executive order has been about, and, it’s the conversation that we’ll continue to have with the community.”

items.author: Gavin Baker
items.text:
Something that merits more discussion amongst those who believe it was a mistake by both the Biden and Trump administrations to allow the export of less powerful GPUs to China:

Since the summer of 2025, it has increasingly been *China*, not just DC, blocking Nvidia GPUs in China. Within weeks of Secretary Lutnick saying the goal was to get Chinese developers "addicted" to the American technology stack, Beijing began pressuring its tech giants to stop buying the H20. Then it ordered them to stop buying the RTX Pro 6000D, sent customs teams to the ports to crack down on Nvidia chip imports, and barred foreign AI chips from new state-funded data centers. And as of last week, Reuters reports that roughly 600,000 H200s are sitting in Hong Kong because Beijing won't approve large-scale imports of a chip that is still better than anything China's own industry makes at scale.

If allowing the export of these less powerful GPUs was a policy mistake that *advantaged* China, then why is *China* the one blocking them?

From my perspective, China understands that if they are dependent on American AI hardware - either on the ground in China or accessed remotely via the wide range of southeast Asian clouds (which include SE Asian availability zones from the largest American hyperscalers) - then we have immense leverage over them in any future conflict. Being able to turn off the clouds instantly is actually the greatest leverage.

Yes, Chinese AI labs still want Nvidia chips. Gray market prices for H200 servers have roughly tripled over the past year. But that is exactly the point. Beijing is willing to impose real costs on its own AI labs to avoid dependence on American GPUs, which tells you how Beijing views GPU imports: not as a gift, but as a threat to its own ambitions.

Maybe, just maybe, selling China GPUs that trail our own state of the art, so that Chinese developers stay “addicted” to American GPUs and China doesn't build an alternative AI hardware ecosystem that we have no control or influence over *and* that China could share over time with our adversaries, was actually a smart, pro-American national defense policy. And letting them access southeast Asian clouds might be an even smarter policy as so easy to turn clouds off.

I believed and still believed it was smart policy. And I say this as someone whose posts here are hawkish enough on China that I won't travel there anymore.

And note that both the Biden and Trump administration allowed the export of less powerful GPUs to China for all of these reasons. It was only under the Trump administration that China woke up to the risk of what was actually a pretty smart, pro-national defense policy and then China began restricting GPUs.

The lesson of the H20 is that a deliberately crippled chip doesn't keep China on our stack. Beijing moved against the H20 and RTX Pro 6000D as it concluded that domestic Chinese chips had caught up to them. So if China develops an alternative AI hardware ecosystem that it shares with Russia, Iran and North Korea, we will look back and think it would have been even smarter to offer China the B30A in 2025 instead of the H200s we eventually approved case-by-case. Especially given the H200 is not the frontier: with Vera Rubin now in full production, it is two generations behind what American labs are buying.

All of this is to say that Jensen has been consistently lobbying for a position that was adapted by both the Biden *and* Trump admins *and* looks smarter every month that goes by as Chinese labs increasingly adapt their MoE architectures to domestic Chinese hardware. DeepSeek reportedly gave Huawei and Cambricon early access to V4 instead of Nvidia and AMD, and a Huawei-led team has since post-trained V4-Pro on Ascend chips.

And if America *ever* falls behind China in AI, the China hawks here in America who helped accelerate the creation of this alternative Chinese AI hardware ecosystem will deserve a significant share of the blame.

items.author: Serenity
items.text:
If you look at CW laser ASPs for AI data centers, the pricing differences are pretty substantial:

70mW: ~$3–4
100mW: ~$4–6 (Source Photonics channel checks).

With some premiums apparently going up to $7-$9 range with the recent shortage for pluggables. 

120–150mW NPO: ~$15–20
350mW UHP CW: ~$40 (Nomura)
400mW UHP CW for NPO/CPO: ~$50–75 (Mizuho)

With former communication laser chips going from 20-50 cents. 

The pricing and gross margins of these players go up with each architectural shift (60%+ for CPO lasers).

And go up even more depending how far down the stack you go (selling ELSFP was ~2.5x revenue content) 

In terms of how I see the landscape now:

- $COHR is probably the best risk adjusted laser player now, for people who don't like uncertainty. Their new $20B LTA is very substantial.

- $LITE pretty negative now given the valuation overhang from $MRVL acquisition. Operationally very opsitive. 

- $AAOI has extreme demand visibility (likely $6-$9B in new LTAs from just 1 quarter), but credible execution uncertainty. 

They've also been focusing on pluggables + bottlenecked by DSPs, rather focusing on UHP CPO laser merchant markets. 

But I think if markets see a new $5B-$7B LTA that they're in late stage discussion for... and see the $4.4B MC. Pretty sure that's a catalyst for recovery. 

The demand doesn't disappear but timeline shifts back a few months. 

AOI also signaled DSP as the main bottleneck, last quarter it was TIAs, so other different component players that are interesting. 

- $SIVE has extreme capacity expansion (300m laser capacity targeted in total). 

The economic implications that they won't disclose are likely enormous relative to their MC, even if they sell $3 70mW lasers to China pluggable players. 

But there's a qualification uncertainty to fill the gap, 
that markets have punished the company for. Especially when management communication amplifies uncertainty, despite the ongoing shortage. 

Right now entire AI trade is going up and down together though.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other.
items.explanation: E could hide something that breaks the rule; 3 breaks it if the other side turns out to be E. 8 can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and K isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it.

items.headline: AI data centres are hunting for used turbines and jet engines
items.summary: Lead times for new gas turbines now stretch to 2030-2031, so utilities and data-centre developers are reviving mothballed machines and converting retired jet engines, Reuters reports. Wood Mackenzie puts worldwide turbine orders above 100 GW against 60-70 GW of yearly production capacity.
items.short: With new gas turbines backordered to 2030, AI data-centre builders are buying used turbines and converted jet engines.

items.headline: Disney and Adobe will build custom AI models for the parks, studio and ESPN
items.summary: Disney and Adobe struck a multi-year deal to co-develop private generative AI models trained on Disney's own IP through Adobe's Firefly Foundry. Work starts with Imagineering's concept design and the StudioLAB innovation hub; Disney says steps that took months now take hours or days.
items.short: Disney and Adobe signed a multi-year deal to build private generative AI models trained on Disney's IP.

items.headline: FDA adds a rare-blindness warning to all GLP-1 drugs
items.summary: The FDA said Monday that makers of GLP-1 drugs, including Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound, must warn of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare optic-nerve condition that can cause sudden, permanent vision loss. The agency found cases for every marketed GLP-1 but could not identify a mechanism.
items.short: The FDA now requires a warning on all GLP-1 drugs about NAION, a rare cause of sudden vision loss.

items.headline: An mRNA treatment got heart muscle to regrow after heart attacks in mice
items.summary: Cambridge researchers used short-lived mRNA to switch on two proteins, Myc and Cyclin T1, so heart muscle cells divided again after a heart attack. Treated mice pumped about 10% more blood per beat, and the gain held at 12 weeks. Larger-animal and human trials come next (Nature Cardiovascular Research).
items.short: A Cambridge mRNA therapy made mouse heart cells divide after a heart attack, improving pumping by about 10%.
